property_summary: For any caller who is the current owner, calling setOwner(x) sets C.owner() to the provided argument x; the mutant instead sets owner to msg.sender, so for some provided x (where x != caller) the mutant violates this rule.

For any caller who is the current owner and any supplied address _owner, calling setOwner(_owner) sets C.owner() to the provided _owner; the mutant instead clears owner to address(0) for some inputs, violating this rule.

For any caller who is the current owner, calling setOwner(x) updates the public owner() to x; the mutant that omits the assignment breaks this by leaving owner() unchanged for some input owner address x.

For any caller who is the current owner, calling setOwner(x) results in owner() == x (the reference assigns the provided _owner); the mutant instead ignores the parameter and sets owner to tx.origin, so for some caller/tx.origin pairs the resulting owner differs.

For any caller address X, when X calls setOwner(Y) on the reference contract C it only succeeds (updates owner) if X equals the current owner (msg.sender check); the mutant using tx.origin instead can be made to update owner when the immediate caller is not the original owner by routing the call through a contract (so the mutant allows a contract caller to bypass owner if tx.origin matches), thus violating the authorization rule for some inputs.

For all callers, only the current owner (msg.sender) can successfully change owner via setOwner; the mutant that uses tx.origin allows an intermediate contract caller to change owner when tx.origin equals the original owner, breaking this invariant for some inputs.

For all callers, only the direct caller equal to the current owner (msg.sender == owner) can successfully change owner via setOwner; the mutant using tx.origin allows a call routed through an intermediate contract to succeed when tx.origin == owner even if msg.sender != owner, so the mutant can change owner for some inputs.

General rule: only the current owner can successfully call setOwner; the mutant inverts the check allowing non-owners and thereby lets a non-owner change owner (so after a non-owner call the owner differs), which breaks the rule.

For all callers, calling setOwner only changes C.owner when the caller is the current owner (i.e., after any call to setOwner by caller A, C.owner() == A iff A was the prior owner); the mutant removing the onlyOwner check allows a non-owner caller to change owner, violating this rule.

For any caller who is the current owner, calling setOwner(...) succeeds (does not revert) and returns true in the reference implementation; the mutant changes the returned boolean to false for some valid owner calls, violating this return-value rule.

For any caller who is the current owner and any _owner address, calling setOwner succeeds and returns true in the reference; the mutant may return false for some inputs because it returns (msg.sender == _owner) instead of a constant true.

For any caller who is the current owner and any destination address, calling setOwner returns true (the reference returns true unconditionally on success); the mutant instead returns false when setting owner to the zero address, so there exist inputs (setting owner to address(0)) where the mutant's returned value differs.
For any caller who is the current owner, calling setOwner(...) succeeds and returns true; the mutant breaks this by returning false when setting owner to address(0).

For every caller who is the current owner, calling setOwner(x) completes (does not revert) and the returned value equals whether the new owner equals the contract's owner after the call (i.e., return indicates that owner was actually set to the provided address); the mutant returns false when setting owner to address(0) even though owner was set to address(0), so it violates that equivalence for some input.

For every caller who is the current owner and for every address a, calling setOwner(a) returns the boolean value true (i.e., the call reports success) if and only if after the call the contract's owner equals a; the mutant violates this by returning false when setting owner to address(0) even though owner becomes address(0).

For any address caller (the current owner) and any target address newOwner, if setOwner(newOwner) completes (does not revert) then the returned bool equals (newOwner != address(0)) is NOT the correct general rule; instead the correct contract always returns true on successful non-reverting calls, while the mutant returns false when newOwner == address(0) — so the invariant: 'when called successfully, setOwner returns true' holds for the reference for all inputs and is violated by the mutant when newOwner == address(0).

For any caller who is the current owner and any address argument, calling setOwner(_addr) always updates C.owner to _addr (returns true after state change); the mutant returns before assigning so there exist inputs where owner is unchanged.
